Cells and References
When a formula refers to another cell, it uses a cell reference. References come in three forms, and the difference matters as soon as you copy a formula:

Relative (A1) adjusts automatically when the formula is copied to another cell.
Absolute ($A$1) stays fixed when copied. The dollar signs lock both the column and the row.
Mixed ($A1 or A$1) locks only the column or only the row.

For example, =A1*2 multiplies the value in A1 by two. Pressing F4 (or Cmd + T on a Mac) while editing a reference cycles through the relative, absolute, and mixed forms.


Ranges
A range is a group of adjacent cells, written as the top-left cell, a colon, and the bottom-right cell. For example, A1:A10 is a single column of ten cells, and A1:C10 is a rectangular block. A range is the Excel equivalent of a list of values, and it is what most functions take as an input. You can reference an entire column with A:A or an entire row with 1:1.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.2 Entering Formulas and Functions
Every calculation in Excel begins with an equals sign (=). A function relates an input (its arguments) to an output. The workflow is always the same: type =, name the function, read the tooltip that Excel shows to remind you of the arguments, fill in the arguments separated by commas, and press Enter. If you are unsure how a function works, click the fx button next to the formula bar for guided help.
The two functions you will reach for first are SUM and AVERAGE. To total the values in cells A2 through A5:
=SUM(A2:A5)
and to average them:
=AVERAGE(A2:A5)
Once a formula is written, you rarely retype it. Select the cell and drag the small square at its bottom-right corner (the fill handle) to copy the formula. Because references are relative by default, copying down makes Excel adjust the row numbers, and copying across makes it adjust the column letters. This is what lets a single formula compute a whole column of results. Many functions also accept a criteria argument that filters the data, such as =AVERAGEIF(A2:A100, ">=1", B2:B100). If a formula cannot be evaluated, Excel returns an error such as #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #N/A, or #REF!.

Order of Operations
Excel evaluates formulas following the standard order of operations: parentheses first, then exponents, then multiplication and division, and finally addition and subtraction. For example, =2^3*2+2 is evaluated as \((2^3) \times 2 + 2 = 18\), and =2+4*5 is evaluated as \(2 + (4 \times 5) = 22\). When in doubt, add parentheses to make the intended order explicit — =(2+4)*5 returns \(30\).


Array Formulas
A few calculations — like a conditional variance — must be entered as array formulas, which operate on an entire range at once. In modern Excel these “spill” automatically, but in older versions you must complete them by pressing Ctrl + Shift + Enter instead of just Enter.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.3 Navigating and Selecting
Moving quickly around a large worksheet is a skill worth practicing. Turning off the grid with View → Gridlines gives a cleaner canvas, especially when building a report or a chart.
The navigation shortcuts below let you move and select without the mouse:

Ctrl + Arrow jumps to the edge of the current block of data in that direction.
Ctrl + Shift + Arrow selects everything from the active cell to the edge of the data — the fastest way to grab a whole column of values.
F2 (fn + F2 on some Macs) toggles the active cell into edit mode so you can see and adjust the formula in place.
Ctrl + Enter fills every cell in a selection with the same formula at once.

When you want to keep headers visible while scrolling, use View → Freeze Panes. View → Split divides the window into independently scrolling panes, and you can Hide rows, columns, or entire sheets you do not want to see.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.4 Range Names
Rather than referring to $B$2:$B$100, you can give a range a memorable name and use it in formulas and charts. There are three ways to create one: select the range and go to Formulas → Define Name; type a name directly into the Name Box and press Enter; or select a block that includes labels and use Formulas → Create from Selection to name each column or row from its header.
Names follow a few rules: they cannot contain spaces, they cannot look like a cell reference (so Q1 is not allowed as a name), and they must begin with a letter or underscore. Use the Name Manager (Formulas → Name Manager) to review, edit, or delete existing names. A well-named range such as Returns makes =AVERAGE(Returns) far easier to read and audit than a raw address.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.5 Data Types
The main data types in Excel are number, text, logical, date, and error.

Number includes integers and decimals. Numbers are right-aligned in a cell by default.
Text represents labels or strings and is left-aligned by default.
Logical values are TRUE or FALSE, usually produced by a comparison.
Date and time values are stored as serial numbers (see below), which is why dates can be added and subtracted.
Error values are the result of an invalid operation, such as dividing by zero.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.6 Working with Dates and Time
Excel stores every date as a serial number: day 1 is January 1, 1900, day 2 is January 2, 1900, and so on. The integer part of the number counts the days since that starting point, while the decimal part represents the time as a fraction of a 24-hour day. So 0 corresponds to 12:00 am, 0.5 corresponds to 12:00 pm, and a value like 44000.75 is a specific date at 6:00 pm.
Because dates are really numbers, the way a cell is formatted determines whether you see 1/1/2024 or 45292. If a calculation returns a date when you wanted a plain number (or vice versa), change the cell’s number format under Home → Number. To pull just the time (the decimal part) out of a date-time value, use MOD with a divisor of \(1\):
=MOD(A1, 1)
Useful date and time functions include =TODAY() and =NOW() for the current date and date-time, =DATE(year, month, day) to build a date, and =YEAR(), =MONTH(), =DAY(), and =WEEKDAY() to extract the parts of a date.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.7 Working with Text
Text functions let you clean and reshape labels — for example, splitting a “Last, First” name into two columns. The most useful ones are:

=TRIM(text) removes extra spaces, leaving only single spaces between words.
=LEN(text) returns the number of characters in the text.
=LEFT(text, n) and =RIGHT(text, n) return the first or last n characters.
=MID(text, start, n) returns n characters beginning at position start.
=SEARCH(find, text) (or =FIND) returns the position of a character or substring; SEARCH is not case-sensitive, FIND is.
=UPPER(text), =LOWER(text), and =PROPER(text) change capitalization.
=SUBSTITUTE(text, old, new) replaces every occurrence of old with new.
=REPLACE(text, start, n, new) replaces n characters starting at a position with new text.

As an example, suppose cell D6 contains Doe, John. The position of the comma is =SEARCH(",", D6), which returns 4. The last name is then =LEFT(D6, SEARCH(",", D6) - 1) → Doe, and the first name is =RIGHT(D6, LEN(D6) - SEARCH(",", D6) - 1) → John. To join text back together, use the ampersand operator: =B6 & " " & A6, or the =CONCAT() function.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.8 Lookup Functions
Lookup functions find a value in a table based on a key. =VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table, column_number, [match]) searches down the first column of a table and returns a value from a column to its right; =HLOOKUP() does the same across the first row. The modern replacement, =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_range, return_range), is more flexible because the lookup and return ranges can be anywhere and it can look left as well as right.
The optional match argument controls exact versus approximate matching. An approximate (binary) search assumes the lookup column is sorted: Excel repeatedly compares the target with the middle value and discards half the list each time, which is very fast on large data sets — but it returns wrong answers if the data is not sorted. For most business lookups you want an exact match.
Lookups also support wildcards in the search text: ? matches any single character (so B?ll matches Ball and Bell), and * matches any number of characters (so B*ll matches Ball, Bell, and Barbell). Use ~ before a ? or * when you need to match the literal character.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.9 Logical and Conditional Functions
The =IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) function returns one of two values depending on whether a condition is met, and IF statements can be nested inside one another. When you have several conditions to check in order, =IFS(test1, value1, test2, value2, ...) is cleaner. The logical helpers =AND(...), =OR(...), and =NOT(...) combine or reverse conditions.
A closely related family aggregates values that meet a condition:

=COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the cells that satisfy a condition, and =COUNTIFS(...) handles several conditions at once.
=SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range) totals the values that meet a condition, and =SUMIFS(...) allows several conditions.
=AVERAGEIF(range, criteria, average_range) averages the values that meet a condition.

When a criterion is a comparison, write it as text in quotes, for example ">2" or ">=1". To rank values, =RANK.AVG(number, range) returns the position of a value within a list (averaging ties). A common use is to highlight the top items in a chart: rank each value, then use a formula such as =IF(rank <= 5, value, NA()) so that only the top five carry a value and the rest return NA().

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.10 OFFSET and MATCH
=MATCH(lookup_value, array, 0) returns the position of a value within a row or column (the 0 requests an exact match). It does not return the value itself — it tells you where the value sits, which you can then feed to another function.
=OFFSET(reference, rows, cols, [height], [width]) returns a range that is a given number of rows and columns away from a starting reference. The optional height and width arguments let it return a whole block rather than a single cell. Combining MATCH (to locate a position) with OFFSET (to retrieve the value at that position) creates flexible lookups; the same idea is often written with INDEX and MATCH.
Because OFFSET can size a range on the fly, it is the key to dynamic ranges. Pairing it with =COUNTA(range) — which counts the non-empty cells — lets you define a named range that automatically grows as you add data. A chart built on that name then updates itself whenever new rows arrive, with no manual re-selection.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.11 Sorting, Filtering, and Dynamic Arrays
The Data → Sort and Data → Filter tools reorder and subset a table interactively. Excel also provides dynamic array functions that return a whole range of results that “spill” into neighboring cells:

=SORT(range) returns the range sorted.
=FILTER(range, condition) returns only the rows that satisfy a condition.
=RANK(number, range) returns the rank of a value.

These combine naturally with the conditional functions. For example, to keep only the years that appear in a second, larger list, you can flag matches with COUNTIF and pass the result to FILTER:
=FILTER(Years, COUNTIF(OtherYears, Years))
COUNTIF returns a 1 for each year found in OtherYears and a 0 otherwise, and FILTER keeps only the rows flagged with a 1.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.12 Importing and Web Data
To bring outside data into Excel you can open a CSV directly with File → Open, or use Data → Get Data → From Text/CSV for control over how columns are separated. Data → Get Data → From Web pulls tables from a web page — for example, stock history from a finance site. Imported data becomes a query; under Data → Queries & Connections (and Data Source Settings) you can refresh it, change the source, or adjust how it loads. Excel’s Stocks and Geography data types can also enrich a plain list of tickers or country names with live fields. When previewing a large import, freeze the header row with View → Freeze Panes and jump to the end with Ctrl + Down or Ctrl + End.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.13 PivotTables
A PivotTable (Insert → PivotTable) automatically summarizes and counts data, making it the primary tool for building frequency and relative frequency distributions. You drag fields into the Rows, Columns, and Values areas, and Excel aggregates the underlying data for you — counting, summing, or averaging — without writing a single formula. PivotTables are used throughout the descriptive statistics chapters; see Descriptive Statistics II for a worked example.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.14 Charts and Visualization
Charts are created from Insert → Charts. Choosing the right type matters: use a bar chart to compare categories and a line chart to show change over time. A good chart maximizes the data-to-ink ratio — that is, it removes anything that does not convey information. In practice that means removing gridlines, adding subtle borders to bars, cleaning up the axes (sensible tick marks and units), placing the title inside the plot, and adding data labels by right-clicking a series and choosing Add Data Labels.
To compare two series, add a second set of values to the chart. When the two series are on very different scales — a count and a percentage, say — plot one of them on a secondary axis using a combo chart (Chart Design → Change Chart Type → Combo). You can highlight a particular bar, such as the maximum or the top few, by adding a helper column that returns the value only for the rows to highlight and NA() for the rest; because Excel does not plot NA(), only the highlighted bars appear, and setting the series overlap to 100% layers them on top of the originals. A dummy variable that switches between 0 and 1 can be plotted as a shaded band to mark periods such as recessions. Once you have styled a chart the way you like, right-click it and choose Save as Template to reuse the formatting later.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.15 The Data Analysis ToolPak
Some analyses — such as regression — require the Analysis ToolPak, an add-in that ships with Excel but is turned off by default. To enable it on Windows, go to File → Options → Add-ins → Manage: Excel Add-ins → Go, check Analysis ToolPak, and click OK. On a Mac, use Tools → Excel Add-ins. Once enabled, the ToolPak appears under Data → Data Analysis and provides one-click tools for descriptive statistics, regression, random number generation, and more.

title: 15  Excel Basics
text:
15.16 Statistical Function Dictionary
The remainder of the chapter lists the statistical Excel functions used in the book, grouped by the chapter in which they first appear. Each is explained in detail, with worked examples, in its home chapter.

General Purpose

=SUM(range) adds all of the numbers in a range.
=COUNT(range) counts the cells that contain numbers, while =COUNTA(range) counts all non-empty cells.
=MIN(range) and =MAX(range) return the smallest and largest values in a range.
=ABS(number) returns the absolute value of a number.
=SQRT(number) returns the square root of a number.
=IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) returns one of two values depending on whether a condition is met.
=AND(...), =OR(...), and =NOT(...) combine or reverse logical conditions.



Tables and Charts (Descriptive Stats II)

PivotTable (Insert → PivotTable) automatically summarizes and counts data, making it the primary tool for building frequency and relative frequency distributions.
=IFS(test1, value1, test2, value2, ...) checks multiple conditions in order and returns the value for the first one that is true. It is used to assign each numerical observation to its class (bin) when building a frequency distribution.



Measures of Central Location (Descriptive Stats III)

=AVERAGE(range) calculates the mean of a range of numbers.
=MEDIAN(range) calculates the median.
=MODE(range) returns the single most frequent value, while =MODE.MULT(range) returns all modes when the data is multimodal.
=SUMPRODUCT(array1, array2) multiplies corresponding values in two ranges and sums the results. Dividing by =SUM(weights) gives the weighted mean.
=GEOMEAN(range) calculates the geometric mean. For rates of change, apply the function to the growth factors (1 + r) and subtract one at the end.
=AVERAGEIF(range, criteria, average_range) calculates the mean of the values that meet a given condition.



Measures of Dispersion (Descriptive Stats IV)

=COUNTIF(range, criteria) counts the number of cells that meet a condition.
=MINIFS(min_range, criteria_range, criteria) and =MAXIFS(max_range, criteria_range, criteria) return the minimum and maximum values filtered by one or more conditions.
=VAR.S(range) calculates the sample variance; =VAR.P(range) calculates the population variance.
=STDEV.S(range) calculates the sample standard deviation (the square root of the sample variance); =STDEV.P(range) calculates the population standard deviation.
=VAR(IF(criteria_range="condition", value_range)) and =STDEV(IF(criteria_range="condition", value_range)) calculate a conditional variance and standard deviation. Excel has no native VARIF or STDEVIF, so these are entered as array formulas.
Coefficient of Variation has no dedicated function; compute it as =STDEV.S(range) / AVERAGE(range).



Measures of Shape and Position (Descriptive Stats V)

=PERCENTILE.INC(array, k) returns the \(k\)th percentile of a range using the formula \(L_p = 1 + k(n-1)\), where \(k\) is expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1. =PERCENTILE.EXC(array, k) uses the alternative formula \(L_p = k(n+1)\).
=QUARTILE.INC(array, quart) returns the five point summary. The argument quart takes values 0 (minimum), 1 (\(Q_1\)), 2 (median), 3 (\(Q_3\)), and 4 (maximum).
=STANDARDIZE(x, mean, std_dev) calculates the z-score for a value. It can also be computed manually as =(x - AVERAGE(range)) / STDEV.S(range).
=SKEW(range) calculates the skewness of a range.
=KURT(range) calculates the excess kurtosis of a range.



Measures of Association (Regression I)

=COVARIANCE.S(array1, array2) calculates the sample covariance between two variables; =COVARIANCE.P() calculates the population covariance.
=CORREL(array1, array2) calculates the correlation coefficient, which is always between \(-1\) and \(1\).
=CORREL(array1, array2)^2 calculates the coefficient of determination \(R^2\) by squaring the correlation coefficient.



Regression (Regression II)

Data Analysis ToolPak → Regression returns the coefficients, \(R^2\), adjusted \(R^2\), standard error, and the ANOVA table in a single output.
=SLOPE(y_range, x_range) and =INTERCEPT(y_range, x_range) return the slope and intercept of a simple regression line.
=FORECAST.LINEAR(x, y_range, x_range) returns the predicted value of \(y\) for a given \(x\).
=RSQ(y_range, x_range) returns the \(R^2\), and =STEYX(y_range, x_range) returns the residual standard error.



Probability Distributions (Probability I–III)

=FACT(number), =COMBIN(n, x), and =PERMUT(n, x) return the factorial, number of combinations, and number of permutations. Use =COMBINA() and =PERMUTATIONA() when repetition is allowed.
=BINOM.DIST(x, n, p, cumulative), =POISSON.DIST(x, mean, cumulative), and =HYPGEOM.DIST(sample_s, number_sample, population_s, number_pop, cumulative) return discrete probabilities (FALSE for the PMF, TRUE for the cumulative distribution). =BINOM.INV(n, p, alpha) returns a binomial quantile.
=NORM.DIST(x, mean, std_dev, cumulative) and =NORM.S.DIST(z, cumulative) return normal probabilities, while =NORM.INV(probability, mean, std_dev) and =NORM.S.INV(probability) return normal quantiles. =EXPON.DIST(x, lambda, cumulative) returns exponential probabilities.

Exercise 1, question 1
Back to the question


The “Title” variable represents the names of books. Therefore, this is a categorical variable.
“Price” represents the cost of each book in a numeric format, making it a numerical variable.
“Year Published” indicates the publication year of each book. It is numerical.
If “Rating” represents a numerical score based on a continuous scale (e.g., average user ratings on a platform like Goodreads), it is numerical because arithmetic operations like averaging or comparing differences are meaningful. If “Rating” represents predefined categories (e.g., “Excellent,” “Good,” “Fair,” “Poor”) or is interpreted as ranks without meaningful differences between values, it would be categorical.




Exercise 1, question 2
Back to the question


The measurement scale is nominal for “Title” since these are labels used to identify each book and do not have a numerical meaning or order.
If “Rating” represents a score (e.g., 4.2, 4.0) given to each book, it is numerical and could be considered interval data because the scale represents a meaningful difference, but it may not have an absolute zero or meaningful ratios (e.g., a book rated 4.0 is not “twice as good” as one rated 2.0).
“Price” is a measurable quantity with a meaningful zero (e.g., a book priced at $0 means it is free), making it ratio data.
“Year” is interval data because the zero point is arbitrary (year 0 does not represent the absence of time) and differences between years are meaningful (e.g., 1897 - 1818 = 79 years).




Exercise 2, question 1
Back to the question

The variable Year is measured on the interval scale because the observations can be ranked, categorized and measured when using this kind of scale. However, there is no true zero point so we cannot calculate meaningful ratios between years.



Exercise 2, question 2
Back to the question

The variable Quarter is measured on the ordinal scale, even though it contains numbers.



Exercise 2, question 3
Back to the question

The variable Deliveries is measured on the ratio scale. It is the strongest level of measurement because it allows us to categorize and rank the data as well as find meaningful differences between observations. Also, with a true zero point, we can interpret the ratios between observations.



Exercise 3
Back to the question


Customer ID: Categorical, Nominal. These are arbitrary labels used only for identification. There is no order or numerical meaning; you can only determine if two IDs are the same or different.
Satisfaction Level: Categorical, Ordinal. The ratings have a clear order (higher numbers indicate greater satisfaction), but the intervals between levels are not necessarily equal (the difference between 4 and 5 may not be perceived the same as between 1 and 2). Ratios are not meaningful.
Visit Duration: Numerical, Ratio. Time in minutes has a true zero (0 minutes means no time spent), equal intervals, and meaningful ratios (e.g., 60 minutes is twice as long as 30 minutes). All arithmetic operations are valid.
Beverage Type: Categorical, Nominal. These are unordered categories/labels for different drinks. You can group or count them, but there is no natural order or numerical relationship between categories like “Latte” and “Tea”.

Exercise 1, question 1
Back to the question

The minimum is \(0\), the first quartile is \(2\), second quartile is \(4\), third quartile is \(8\), and maximum is \(30\). \(30\) is an outlier since it is beyond \(Q_{3}+1.5 \times IQR\).
Quartiles are calculated with the location formula \(L_p = 1 + k(n-1)\). The sorted data is \(\{0,1,3,4,6,10,30\}\) with \(n = 7\):

\(L_{25} = 1 + 0.25(6) = 2.5 \Rightarrow Q_1 = 1 + 0.5(3-1) = 2\)
\(L_{50} = 1 + 0.50(6) = 4 \Rightarrow Median = 4\)
\(L_{75} = 1 + 0.75(6) = 5.5 \Rightarrow Q_3 = 6 + 0.5(10-6) = 8\)

In Excel we get the five point summary with =QUARTILE.INC():
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 0)   /* Minimum = 0  */
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 1)   /* Q1      = 2  */
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 2)   /* Median  = 4  */
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 3)   /* Q3      = 8  */
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 4)   /* Maximum = 30 */
The interquartile range is needed to determine if there are any outliers. The \(IQR = Q_3 - Q_1 = 6\). Since \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times IQR = 8 + 1.5(6) = 17\), everything beyond \(17\) is an outlier, so \(30\) is an outlier.
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 3) - QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 1)   /* IQR = 6  */
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 3) + 1.5 * 6                 /* UL  = 17 */



Exercise 1, question 2
Back to the question

If we use the \(z\)-score instead we find that \(30\) is not an outlier since the \(z\)-score is \(Z_{30}=2.15\). This observation is only \(2.15\) standard deviations away from the mean.
In Excel we make a quick calculation of the \(z\)-score to confirm our result. The \(z\)-score is \(Z_{i}=\frac{x_{i}-\bar{x}}{s}\):
=STANDARDIZE(30, AVERAGE(A:A), STDEV.S(A:A))   /* = 2.15 */
Since \(2.15 < 3\), the value \(30\) is not flagged as an outlier by the \(z\)-score method, even though the IQR method flagged it. The two methods can disagree.



Exercise 1, question 3
Back to the question

Chebyshev’s theorem states that \(1-\frac{1}{z^{2}}\) of the data lies between \(z\) standard deviations from the mean.
Substituting the \(z\)-score found in 2. we get that at least \(78.34\%\) of the data lies within that many standard deviations of the mean. In Excel:
=1 - 1/(2.15^2)    /* ≈ 0.7834, i.e. 78.34% */

Exercise 2, question 1
Back to the question

From the multiplication rule, \[P(A|B)*P(B)=P(A \cap B)\]
substituting values yields: \[P(A \cap B)=0.45*0.3=0.135\] From the addition rule, \[P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)\] substituting yields: \[P(A \cup B)=0.65+0.3-0.135=0.815\] From the multiplication rule once again, \[P(B|A)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}\] substituting values yields, \[P(B|A)=0.135/0.65=0.2076923\]



Exercise 2, question 2
Back to the question

From the complement rule we have that \(P(A^c)=0.6\) and \(P(B^c)=0.5\).
Using the multiplication rule, \[P(A^c|B^c)=\frac{P(A^c \cap B^c)}{P(B^c)}\] substituting yields: \[P(A^c|B^c)=0.24/0.5=0.48\] From the addition rule, \[P(A^c \cup B^c)=P(A^c)+P(B^c)-P(A^c \cap B^c)\] substituting yields: \[P(A^c \cup B^c)=0.6+0.5-0.24=0.86\] The event that has no elements of \(A\) or \(B\) is given by \(P(A^c \cap B^c)\). Therefore \(P(A \cup B)=1-0.24=0.76\) has all the elements of A and B.



Exercise 2, question 3
Back to the question

In short, the problem states \(P(A)=0.4\), \(P(B)=0.6\), and \(P(A|B)=0.5\). Where \(A\) and \(B\) are events of stocks rising in price. The question asks for: \[P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)\] Using the multiplication rule, \[P(A \cap B)=0.5*0.6=0.3\] Hence, \[P(A \cup B)=0.4+0.6-0.3=0.7\] The events are not mutually exclusive since \(P(A \cap B)=0.3 \neq 0\). The events are also not independent since \(P(A|B)=0.5 \neq 0.4=P(A)\).



Exercise 3, question 1
Back to the question

Rearranging the addition rule, \[P(A \cap B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cup B)=0.5+0.4-0.7=0.2\] Using the conditional probability formula, \[P(A|B)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}=\frac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5 \qquad P(B|A)=\frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}=\frac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4\] The events are not mutually exclusive since \(P(A \cap B)=0.2 \neq 0\). They are independent since \(P(A|B)=0.5=P(A)\) (equivalently, \(P(A)P(B)=0.5 \times 0.4=0.2=P(A \cap B)\)).



Exercise 3, question 2
Back to the question

Since the events are independent, \[P(A \cap B)=P(A)P(B)=0.3 \times 0.6=0.18\] From the addition rule, \[P(A \cup B)=0.3+0.6-0.18=0.72\] Independence also means that knowing \(B\) happened does not change the probability of \(A\), so \(P(A|B)=P(A)=0.3\). Finally, by De Morgan’s law, \(A^c \cap B^c=(A \cup B)^c\), so \[P(A^c \cap B^c)=1-P(A \cup B)=1-0.72=0.28\] As a check, the complements of independent events are also independent: \(P(A^c)P(B^c)=0.7 \times 0.4=0.28\).



Exercise 3, question 3
Back to the question

Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together, so \(P(A \cap B)=0\). The addition rule then simplifies to \[P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)=0.25+0.45=0.70\] Since \(A\) and \(B\) never occur together, \(P(A|B)=0/0.45=0\). The probability that neither occurs is the complement of the union: \(1-0.70=0.30\).
The events are not independent. If \(B\) happens, the probability of \(A\) drops from \(0.25\) to \(0\), so knowing \(B\) changes the probability of \(A\). Mutually exclusive events (with positive probabilities) are always dependent.



Exercise 3, question 4
Back to the question

In short, \(P(M)=0.60\), \(P(P)=0.05\), and \(P(M \cap P)=0.02\). From the addition rule, \[P(M \cup P)=0.60+0.05-0.02=0.63\] The probability that a mobile visitor buys is \[P(P|M)=\frac{P(M \cap P)}{P(M)}=\frac{0.02}{0.60}=0.033\] Visitors who do not use a mobile phone make up \(P(M^c)=0.40\) of the traffic, and they account for the remaining \(0.05-0.02=0.03\) of purchases, so \[P(P|M^c)=\frac{0.03}{0.40}=0.075\] Purchasing is not independent of the device: \(P(P|M)=0.033 \neq 0.05=P(P)\). Desktop visitors are more than twice as likely to buy as mobile visitors.



Exercise 3, question 5
Back to the question

Since the failures are independent, \[P(\text{both fail})=0.02 \times 0.02=0.0004\] “At least one is working” is the complement of “both fail”: \[P(\text{at least one works})=1-0.0004=0.9996\] “Exactly one fails” can happen in two mutually exclusive ways: the first fails and the second works, or the first works and the second fails. Adding them, \[P(\text{exactly one fails})=(0.02)(0.98)+(0.98)(0.02)=0.0392\]

Exercise 5, question 2
Back to the question

a) The probability of a Head-On crash is:
\[P(\text{Head-on})=\frac{166+108}{4858}=\frac{274}{4858}=0.056\]
b) The probability that the crash is in daylight is:

Exercise 6, question 1
Back to the question

\(P(A^c)=1-P(A)=1-0.7=0.3\), \(P(A \cap B)=𝑃(𝐵|𝐴)𝑃(𝐴) = 0.55(0.70) = 0.385\), \(P(A^c \cap B)=𝑃(B|A^c)𝑃(A^c) = 0.10(0.30) = 0.03\), \(P(B)= 𝑃(A \cap B) + 𝑃(𝐴^c \cap 𝐵) = 0.385 + 0.03 = 0.415\), and \(P(A|B)= \frac{𝑃(A \cap B)}{P(B)}=0.385/0.415=0.9277\).



Exercise 6, question 2
Back to the question

Let the event of failing be \(F\), the event of not failing be \(NF\), the event of having a tutor be \(T\), and the event of not having a tutor be \(NT\). The probability of failing the course is \(0.25\). \((𝐹) = 𝑃(𝐹 \cap 𝑇) + 𝑃(𝐹 \cap 𝑇^c) = 𝑃(𝐹|𝑇)𝑃(𝑇) + 𝑃(𝐹|𝑇^c)𝑃(𝑇^c) = 0.10(0.50) + 0.40(0.50) = 0.05 + 0.20 = 0.25\) The probability of not having a tutor, given that she failed the course is \(0.2\). \(P(𝑇|𝐹) = \frac{𝑃(𝐹\cap𝑇)}{𝑃(𝐹\cap𝑇)+𝑃(𝐹 \cap𝑇^c)}= 0.05/0.25 = 0.20\).

Back to the question

\(3!=3 \times 2 \times 1=6\), \(4!=4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1=24\), \(C_6^8=28\), and \(P_6^8=20{,}160\).
In Excel:

=FACT(3) → \(6\)
=FACT(4) → \(24\)
=COMBIN(8, 6) → \(28\)
=PERMUT(8, 6) → \(20{,}160\)




Exercise 7, question 2
Back to the question

If order doesn’t matter, there are \(252\) ways. If order matters, then there are \(30{,}240\) ways.
In Excel:

=COMBIN(10, 5) → \(252\)
=PERMUT(10, 5) → \(30{,}240\)




Exercise 7, question 3
Back to the question

The order in which the two people are picked does not matter, so we count combinations. The number of possible pairs is \[C_2^6=\frac{6!}{2!\,4!}=15\] Every pair is equally likely, so we can use the classical method. The number of pairs made up of two analysts is \(C_2^4=6\), so \[P(\text{both analysts})=\frac{6}{15}=0.4\] “At least one intern” is the complement of “both analysts”: \[P(\text{at least one intern})=1-0.4=0.6\] We can check this by counting directly: there are \(C_1^4 \times C_1^2=8\) pairs with one analyst and one intern, and \(C_2^2=1\) pair with both interns, so \((8+1)/15=0.6\).
In Excel:

=COMBIN(6, 2) → \(15\)
=COMBIN(4, 2)/COMBIN(6, 2) → \(0.4\)
=1 - COMBIN(4, 2)/COMBIN(6, 2) → \(0.6\)

Exercise 1, question 1
Back to the question

The expected value is \(10.75\) and the standard deviation is \(5.31\). The probability of \(x<15\) is \(0.65\).
In Excel, enter the values x in column A and the probabilities P(X=x) in column B:

=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A5, B2:B5) → \(10.75\) (expected value)

Exercise 1, question 2
Back to the question

The expected value is \(-17.4\) and the standard deviation is \(6.86\). The probability of \(x \geq -9\) is \(0.25\).
In Excel, with y in column A and P(Y=y) in column B:

=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A5, B2:B5) → \(-17.4\)
=SQRT(SUMPRODUCT((A2:A5-(-17.4))^2, B2:B5)) → \(6.86\)

Exercise 1, question 3
Back to the question

Both funds have the same expected return of \(6\). The safest return comes from fund 1 since the standard deviation is only \(11.14\) vs. \(31.05\) for fund 2.
In Excel, enter the probabilities in column A, Fund 1 in column B, and Fund 2 in column C:

=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A4, B2:B4) → \(6\) (Fund 1 expected return)
=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A4, C2:C4) → \(6\) (Fund 2 expected return)
=SQRT(SUMPRODUCT((B2:B4-6)^2, A2:A4)) → \(11.14\) (Fund 1 std. dev.)
=SQRT(SUMPRODUCT((C2:C4-6)^2, A2:A4)) → \(31.05\) (Fund 2 std. dev.)

Since both funds have the same expected return, choose Fund 1 — it achieves that return with much less risk.



Exercise 2, question 1
Back to the question

The portfolio weights are \(\alpha=2/5=0.4\) for X and \(\beta=3/5=0.6\) for Y. In Excel:

Standard deviation \(\sqrt{\alpha^2 \sigma_1^2+\beta^2 \sigma_2^2+2\alpha\beta\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}\): =SQRT(0.4^2*12^2 + 0.6^2*20^2 + 2*0.4*0.6*0.4*12*20) → \(14.60\)

Back to the question

\(P(Z=1)=0.31\), and \(P(Z \geq 2)=0.57\). The expected value is \(np=1.75\) and the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{np(1-p)}=1.067\).

Back to the question

Exercise 3, question 3
Back to the question

The probabilities are the same. Each event has a probability of \(0.3456\). If the probability changes to \(0.5\) now the event of two women and two men is more likely.
In Excel:

=BINOM.DIST(3, 4, 0.6, FALSE) → \(0.3456\) (three men)
=BINOM.DIST(2, 4, 0.6, FALSE) → \(0.3456\) (two men)
=BINOM.DIST(3, 4, 0.5, FALSE) → \(0.25\)

Back to the question

The \(P(S=2)=0.25\) and \(P(S \geq 2)=0.44\). The expected value and the variance is \(1.5\).

Exercise 4, question 2
Back to the question

The \(P(T=14)=0.039\) and \(P(18 \leq T \leq 23)=0.49\).
In Excel:

Exercise 4, question 3
Back to the question

The probability of administering more than \(8\) but less than \(12\) shots is \(0.3\).
If \(84\) shots are administered on average weekly, then \(12\) are administered daily. Using this daily mean in Excel:

=POISSON.DIST(11, 12, TRUE) - POISSON.DIST(8, 12, TRUE) → \(0.30\)




Exercise 5, question 1
Back to the question

\(P(X=0)=0.58\), \(P(X=1)=0.37\), and \(P(X \leq 1)=0.94\).
In Excel (successes in population \(r=3\), population \(N=25\), sample \(n=4\)):

=HYPGEOM.DIST(1, 4, 3, 25, FALSE) → \(0.37\)

Exercise 5, question 2
Back to the question

The probability is \(0.078\).

=1 - HYPGEOM.DIST(7, 20, 25, 100, TRUE) → \(0.078\)




Exercise 5, question 3
Back to the question

The probability of matching two white balls is \(5\%\). Winning the jackpot is extremely unlikely! A probability of \(0.00000000512\). It is more likely to be struck by lightning according to the CDC.
In Excel, treat the five drawn white balls as the successes in a population of \(59\), with the player’s five picks as the sample:

=HYPGEOM.DIST(2, 5, 5, 59, FALSE) → \(0.05\) (match two white balls)

For the jackpot, multiply the probability of matching all five white balls by the probability of matching the single Powerball (1 of 39):

=HYPGEOM.DIST(5, 5, 5, 59, FALSE) * HYPGEOM.DIST(1, 1, 1, 39, FALSE) → \(0.00000000512\)

Exercise 1, question 1
Back to the question

The height of the density function \(f(x)=0.1667\), the mean is \(1\), standard deviation is \(1.73\), and \(P(X \leq -1)=0.1667\).
The uniform distribution has no Excel function, so each quantity is computed directly from its formula:

Height \(f(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}\): =1/(4-(-2)) → \(0.1667\)
Mean \(\mu=\frac{a+b}{2}\): =(-2+4)/2 → \(1\)
Standard deviation \(\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}}\): =SQRT((4-(-2))^2/12) → \(1.73\)
\(P(X \leq -1)=\frac{x-a}{b-a}\): =(-1-(-2))/(4-(-2)) → \(0.1667\)

Back to the question

The probability that you will arrive on time is \(0.875\). If the time of the errand is 30 minutes, then the probability goes down to \(0.75\).
There is a \(120\) minute interval in which the provider can arrive, so \(P(X>t)=1-\frac{t}{120}\). In Excel:

=1 - 15/120 → \(0.875\)
=1 - 30/120 → \(0.75\)

Back to the question

\(P(-0.67 \leq Z \leq -0.23)=0.158\), \(P(0 \leq Z \leq 1.96)=0.475\), \(P(-1.28 \leq Z \leq 0)=0.4\) and \(P(Z > 4.2) \approx 0\).
Use the =NORM.S.DIST() function for the standard normal distribution:

=NORM.S.DIST(-0.23, TRUE) - NORM.S.DIST(-0.67, TRUE) → \(0.158\)
=NORM.S.DIST(1.96, TRUE) - NORM.S.DIST(0, TRUE) → \(0.475\)
=NORM.S.DIST(0, TRUE) - NORM.S.DIST(-1.28, TRUE) → \(0.4\)

Back to the question

\(P(Y>7.6)=0.005386\), \(P(7.4 \leq Y \leq 10.6)=0.0071\), a \(y\) such that \(P(Y>y)=0.025\) is \(6.42\), and a \(y\) such that \(P(y \leq Y \leq 2.5)\) is \(-2.56\).
Use =NORM.DIST() for probabilities and =NORM.INV() for quantiles:

=1 - NORM.DIST(7.6, 2.5, 2, TRUE) → \(0.005386\)
=NORM.DIST(10.6, 2.5, 2, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(7.4, 2.5, 2, TRUE) → \(0.0071\)

Since \(2.5\) is the mean, \(P(y \leq Y \leq 2.5)=0.4943\) leaves \(0.5-0.4943=0.0057\) in the left tail: =NORM.INV(0.0057, 2.5, 2) → \(-2.56\)

Back to the question

Back to the question

11 Inference I

Exercise 1, question 1
Back to the question


In a modern version of Excel, type the following in the top-left cell of an empty block; it will spill into a \(10 \times 1000\) grid where each column is a sample of size \(10\):

=RANDARRAY(10, 1000, 100, 200, FALSE)

In an older version, enter =100 + 100*RAND() in the top-left cell and copy it across \(1000\) columns and down \(10\) rows.
Because the values are drawn from a uniform distribution on \([100, 200]\), the population mean is \(\mu = \frac{100+200}{2} = 150\) and the population standard deviation is \(\sigma = \frac{200-100}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 28.87\). (The values recalculate on every edit; to freeze a sample, copy the block and use Paste Special → Values.)




Exercise 1, question 2
Back to the question


Below the block, compute the mean of each column and copy it across all \(1000\) columns:

=AVERAGE(A1:A10) → the mean of the first sample

This produces \(1000\) sample means. Summarize them with:

=AVERAGE(...) → about \(150\), matching the population mean (unbiasedness)
=STDEV.S(...) → about \(9.1\)

The standard deviation of the sample means is far smaller than the population standard deviation (\(\approx 28.87\)), and it matches the standard error \(\sigma / \sqrt{n} = 28.87 / \sqrt{10} \approx 9.13\).




Exercise 1, question 3
Back to the question


Select the \(1000\) sample means and go to Insert → Charts → Histogram (or use the bins-and-PivotTable method from Descriptive Statistics II). Although the population is uniform, the distribution of the sample means is bell-shaped — this is the Central Limit Theorem in action.
Using a normal distribution with mean \(150\) and standard error \(9.13\):

=NORM.DIST(160, 150, 9.13, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(140, 150, 9.13, TRUE) → about \(0.73\)

There is roughly a \(73\%\) probability that the sample mean falls between \(140\) and \(160\). Because the numbers are random, your exact value will vary slightly each time the sheet recalculates.




Exercise 2, question 1
Back to the question


The expected value is \(80\) (equal to the population mean). The standard error is \(1.4\), and the probability is \(98.38\%\).
In Excel:

=14/SQRT(100) → \(1.4\) (standard error)
=NORM.DIST(85, 80, 1.4, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(77, 80, 1.4, TRUE) → \(0.9838\)

title: 8  Probability I
text:
Frequentist view. A probability is the long-run proportion of times an event occurs when an experiment is repeated many times under the same conditions. Saying a product has a \(2\%\) return rate means that, over many sales, about \(2\) in every \(100\) items come back. In this view, probabilities only make sense for events that can be repeated.
Bayesian view. A probability is a degree of belief about how likely an event is. It is subjective in the sense that it reflects a reasoned judgment based on the evidence and experience available, not a random guess, and it is updated as new data arrive. This lets us put a probability on one-time events, such as the chance that a particular product launch succeeds. A frequentist would not assign such a probability, because the launch cannot be repeated.



Example: A company estimates the return rate of an existing product from the share of past sales that were returned. That is a frequentist probability. For a brand-new product with no sales history, managers instead assign a probability of success from market research and experience, and revise it as early sales come in. That is a Bayesian probability.

title: 8  Probability I
text:
8.4 Probability Requirements
Whichever method we use to assign them, probabilities must satisfy two requirements. Any set of numbers that breaks either one is not a valid set of probabilities.

THE TWO REQUIREMENTS OF PROBABILITY

Every probability is between \(0\) and \(1\): \[0 \leq P(A) \leq 1\]
The probabilities of a set of mutually exclusive and exhaustive outcomes add up to \(1\): \[\sum P(x_i) = 1\] where \(x_i\) is outcome \(i\).



Requirement 1: From Certainty to Uncertainty
The two ends of the scale represent certainty. A probability of \(0\) means the event is impossible, and a probability of \(1\) means it is certain to happen. In both cases there is nothing left to guess.
Everything in between is uncertainty. The closer a probability is to \(0.5\), the less we know: at \(0.5\) the event is as likely to happen as not, like a coin flip. A probability of \(0.95\) or \(0.05\) still leaves some doubt, but we can act with a lot of confidence.
Information moves probabilities toward the extremes. As we learn more, we can say with greater confidence whether something will or will not happen. This is why businesses collect data: good information reduces uncertainty.


  
    
  
  
  
    
    
    0.10
    no information yet
    
    
    0.70
    missed three payments
    
    
    0.02
    excellent credit history
    
    0 · impossible
    0.5 · most uncertain
    1 · certain
  



Example: A bank is deciding whether to approve a loan. Before it knows anything about the applicant, it uses the default rate for all borrowers, so \(P(\text{default}) = 0.10\). If the applicant has an excellent credit history, the estimate drops to about \(0.02\), close to certain the loan will be repaid. If instead the applicant has missed three payments on other loans, it rises to about \(0.70\), much closer to certain default. In each case, new information pushed the probability away from the uncertain middle and toward one of the extremes. Once the loan is fully repaid, the uncertainty is gone: \(P(\text{default}) = 0\).



Requirement 2: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Outcomes
The second requirement is about how the probabilities of different outcomes fit together.

Mutually exclusive events do not share any outcomes: if one happens, the others cannot.
Exhaustive events cover every outcome in the sample space: one of them must happen.

When a list of events is both mutually exclusive and exhaustive, exactly one of them will occur. Their probabilities must therefore add up to \(1\): something must happen, and only one thing can.

Example: Consider the four suits in a deck of cards (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades). They are mutually exclusive, because a card cannot belong to two suits, and exhaustive, because every card belongs to one of them. Their probabilities add up to \(1\):
\[P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{diamonds}) + P(\text{clubs}) + P(\text{spades}) = 4 \times \frac{13}{52} = 1\]
Both conditions matter. Hearts and spades alone are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, so \(P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{spades}) = 0.5\) falls short of \(1\). Hearts and red cards are not mutually exclusive, since every heart is also red, so adding \(P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{red}) = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75\) counts the hearts twice.

title: 8  Probability I
text:
8.4 Basic Requirements for Assigning Probabilities
Whichever method we use to assign probabilities (classical, relative frequency, or subjective), the result must satisfy two basic requirements. Any set of numbers that breaks either one is not a valid set of probabilities.

BASIC REQUIREMENTS FOR ASSIGNING PROBABILITIES

Every probability is between \(0\) and \(1\): \[0 \leq P(A) \leq 1\]
The probabilities of all the outcomes in the sample space add up to \(1\): \[\sum P(x_i) = 1\] where \(x_i\) is outcome \(i\) of the experiment.



Requirement 1: From Certainty to Uncertainty
The two ends of the scale represent certainty. A probability of \(0\) means the event is impossible, and a probability of \(1\) means it is certain to happen. In both cases there is nothing left to guess.
Everything in between is uncertainty. The closer a probability is to \(0.5\), the less we know: at \(0.5\) the event is as likely to happen as not, like a coin flip. A probability of \(0.95\) or \(0.05\) still leaves some doubt, but we can act with a lot of confidence.
Information moves probabilities toward the extremes. As we learn more, we can say with greater confidence whether something will or will not happen. This is why businesses collect data: good information reduces uncertainty.


  
    
  
  
  
    
    0.10
    no information yet
    
    0.70
    missed three payments
    
    0.02
    excellent credit history
    0 · impossible
    0.5 · most uncertain
    1 · certain
  



Example: A bank is deciding whether to approve a loan. Before it knows anything about the applicant, it uses the default rate for all borrowers, so \(P(\text{default}) = 0.10\). If the applicant has an excellent credit history, the estimate drops to about \(0.02\), close to certain the loan will be repaid. If instead the applicant has missed three payments on other loans, it rises to about \(0.70\), much closer to certain default. In each case, new information pushed the probability away from the uncertain middle and toward one of the extremes. Once the loan is fully repaid, the uncertainty is gone: \(P(\text{default}) = 0\).



Requirement 2: The Probabilities Add Up to 1
When we run an experiment, one of its outcomes must occur. The probability that something in the sample space happens is therefore \(1\), and that total has to be shared among the outcomes. If the probabilities added up to less than \(1\), we would be leaving room for nothing to happen; if they added up to more, we would be counting some possibility more than once.
The outcomes of an experiment have two properties that make this work:

They are mutually exclusive: they do not overlap, so if one happens the others cannot.
They are exhaustive: together they cover every possibility in the sample space, so one of them must happen.

The same logic applies to any list of events, not just individual outcomes. Whenever a list of events is both mutually exclusive and exhaustive, exactly one of them will occur, so their probabilities add up to \(1\): something must happen, and only one thing can.

Example: Consider the four suits in a deck of cards (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades). They are mutually exclusive, because a card cannot belong to two suits, and exhaustive, because every card belongs to one of them. Their probabilities add up to \(1\):
\[P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{diamonds}) + P(\text{clubs}) + P(\text{spades}) = 4 \times \frac{13}{52} = 1\]
Both conditions matter. Hearts and spades alone are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, so \(P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{spades}) = 0.5\) falls short of \(1\). Hearts and red cards are not mutually exclusive, since every heart is also red, so adding \(P(\text{hearts}) + P(\text{red}) = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75\) counts the hearts twice.

title: 1  Descriptive Stats I
text:
1.5 Check Your Understanding
Test the main ideas of the chapter before moving on to the exercises. Pick an answer to see whether you are right and why.

A retailer records the total revenue of each of its \(50\) stores on Black Friday 2025. What kind of data is this?

Time series data
Cross-sectional data
Unstructured data
Ordinal data


The data cover many stores at a single point in time. If the retailer tracked one store’s revenue week after week, it would be time series data.



A company collects thousands of customer reviews written on social media. How would you classify this data?

Structured data, because it can be counted
Time series data, because reviews have dates
Cross-sectional numerical data
Unstructured data


Free text does not fit a predefined row-and-column format, so it is unstructured. It must be processed (for example, turned into ratings or word counts) before it can be analyzed like a spreadsheet.



In the electric vehicle data set, each row is a car model and one of the columns is Range_km. What is Range_km?

A variable
An element
An observation
A data set


Variables are the characteristics measured for every element, and they appear as columns. The elements are the car models (the rows), and an observation is one car’s full set of values.



Customers rate their satisfaction from 1 (very poor) to 5 (excellent). Which scale of measurement is this?

Nominal
Interval
Ordinal
Ratio


The order is meaningful (a 4 is better than a 3), but the gaps between ratings are not guaranteed to be equal, so the data are ordinal even though they are written as numbers.



The players on a soccer team wear jersey numbers. Which scale of measurement are the jersey numbers?

Ordinal
Interval
Ratio
Nominal


The numbers are only labels that identify each player. Number 10 is not “more” than number 5, and averaging jersey numbers would be meaningless.



Why is temperature in degrees Fahrenheit measured on an interval scale and not a ratio scale?

Because temperatures can include decimals
Because \(0^\circ\)F does not mean “no heat”
Because the order of temperatures does not matter
Because the differences between temperatures are not meaningful


On an interval scale the zero is arbitrary. Since \(0^\circ\)F is not the absence of heat, \(80^\circ\)F is not “twice as hot” as \(40^\circ\)F, even though the \(40\)-degree difference is meaningful.



Which summary statistic makes sense for a nominal variable such as car Brand?

The mean
The median
The mode
The standard deviation


With nominal data we can only count how often each category appears, so the most common category (the mode) is the natural summary. The median needs an order and the mean needs numbers with equal gaps.



Which statement can only be made about data measured on a ratio scale?

One value is twice as large as another
One value is larger than another
The difference between two values is 20 units
The values fall into distinct categories


Ratios need a true zero. A price of $20 is twice a price of $10, but the year 2020 is not twice the year 1010. Ordering works from the ordinal scale up, and differences work from the interval scale up.

title: 2  Descriptive Stats II
text:
2.6 Check Your Understanding
Test the main ideas of the chapter before moving on to the exercises. Pick an answer to see whether you are right and why.

A store manager tallies how many customers paid with cash, debit card, credit card, or a phone wallet. Which graph best displays this frequency distribution?

A histogram
A scatter plot
A bar chart
A line chart


Payment method is categorical, so a bar chart with gaps between the bars is the right choice. Histograms are for numerical data grouped into classes.



In a survey of \(40\) customers, \(10\) said email is their preferred contact method. What is the relative frequency of email?

\(0.25\)
\(10\)
\(0.40\)
\(4\)


The relative frequency is the class frequency divided by the number of observations: \(10/40=0.25\), or \(25\%\).



A data set has \(100\) observations. How many classes does the \(2^k\) rule suggest?

\(6\)
\(5\)
\(10\)
\(7\)


We need the smallest \(k\) with \(2^k\) greater than \(100\). Since \(2^6=64\) falls short and \(2^7=128\) exceeds \(100\), we use \(7\) classes.



For the same \(100\) observations, how many classes does Sturges’ rule suggest?

\(7\)
\(8\)
\(6\)
\(10\)


\(k=\lceil 1+3.322\log_{10}(100)\rceil=\lceil 1+3.322(2)\rceil=\lceil 7.644\rceil=8\). The two rules can disagree, and either one is acceptable if you apply it consistently.



A numerical variable has a minimum of \(12\) and a maximum of \(90\). You want \(5\) classes and a whole-number width. Which width should you use?

\(16\)
\(15\)
\(78\)
\(15.6\)


The width is \((90-12)/5=15.6\), and we always round up, so \(16\). A width of \(15\) would make the last class end at \(12+5(15)=87\), leaving the maximum of \(90\) out.



Which values belong to the class \([20,30)\)?

Values above \(20\) up to and including \(30\)
Values from \(20\) to \(30\), both included
Values from \(20\) up to, but not including, \(30\)
Values strictly between \(20\) and \(30\)


The square bracket includes the endpoint and the parenthesis excludes it. A value of exactly \(30\) goes in the next class, \([30,40)\), so every value belongs to exactly one class.



What is the key visual difference between a histogram and a bar chart?

A histogram can only show relative frequencies
The bars of a histogram touch because the classes cover a continuous numerical range
Bar charts are used for numerical data and histograms for categorical data
A histogram has wider gaps between its bars


In Excel we set the gap width to \(0\%\) to turn the column chart into a histogram. Touching bars signal numerical data, while gaps signal separate categories.



In the Dow Jones frequency distribution, the class \([220,320)\) has a cumulative percentage of \(86.67\%\). What does this mean?

\(86.67\%\) of the stock prices fall in \([220,320)\)
\(86.67\%\) of the stock prices are above \(220\)
\(13.33\%\) of the stock prices are below \(320\)
\(86.67\%\) of the stock prices are below \(320\)


A cumulative percentage is a running total. The first three classes hold \(9+12+5=26\) of the \(30\) prices, and \(26/30=86.67\%\).

title: 3  Descriptive Statistics III
text:
3.10 Check Your Understanding
Test the main ideas of the chapter before moving on to the exercises. Pick an answer to see whether you are right and why.

Five employees earn \(40\), \(45\), \(50\), \(55\), and \(500\) thousand dollars. Which measure best describes the typical salary?

The mean, because it uses every value
The mode, because salaries are numerical
The geometric mean, because salaries are rates
The median, because the \(500\) does not pull it


The mean is \(690/5=138\) thousand, far above what four of the five employees earn. The median, \(50\) thousand, is resistant to the outlier.



What is the median of \(x=\{2, 9, 4, 12\}\)?

\(6.75\)
\(6.5\)
\(9\)
\(4\)


Sort the data: \(\{2,4,9,12\}\). With \(n=4\) (even), the median is the average of the two middle values, \((4+9)/2=6.5\). The value \(6.75\) is the mean.



A dealership records the brand of each car sold this month. Which measure of central location can it use?

The mode
The mean
The median
The geometric mean


Brand is a categorical variable with no numerical values or natural order, so the only meaningful center is the most frequent brand.



What is the mode of \(x=\{2, 5, 5, 8, 8, 10\}\)?

Only \(8\)
Only \(5\)
\(5\) and \(8\); the data are bimodal
There is no mode


Both \(5\) and \(8\) appear twice, more than any other value, so the data have two modes. Note that Excel’s =MODE() would return only one of them.



A portfolio puts \(60\%\) of its money in a fund that returned \(5\%\) and \(40\%\) in a fund that returned \(10\%\). What is the portfolio’s weighted mean return?

\(7.5\%\)
\(7\%\)
\(15\%\)
\(6\%\)


\(\bar{x}_w=\frac{0.6(5)+0.4(10)}{0.6+0.4}=3+4=7\%\). The simple average, \(7.5\%\), ignores that more money sits in the lower-return fund.



An investment gains \(50\%\) in year one and loses \(50\%\) in year two. What is its average annual return?

\(0\%\)
\(25\%\)
\(-50\%\)
About \(-13.4\%\)


Use the geometric mean for rates: \(\sqrt{1.5 \times 0.5}-1=\sqrt{0.75}-1\approx-0.134\). A $100 investment grows to $150 and then falls to $75, so it clearly lost money. The arithmetic mean of \(0\%\) overstates the result.



Weights are in B2:B5 and values in C2:C5. Which Excel formula returns the weighted mean?

=SUMPRODUCT(B2:B5, C2:C5)/SUM(B2:B5)
=AVERAGE(C2:C5)
=SUMPRODUCT(B2:B5, C2:C5)/4
=GEOMEAN(B2:B5, C2:C5)


SUMPRODUCT multiplies each value by its weight and adds the products. Dividing by the sum of the weights completes the formula \(\sum w_i x_i / \sum w_i\).



When should you use the population mean formula \(\mu=\sum x_i/N\)?

When the data are a subset drawn from a larger group
Whenever the data set has more than \(30\) observations
When the data include every member of the group you care about
Only when the data are categorical


Population formulas apply when you observe the entire group. When the data are a sample from a larger population, you compute the sample statistic \(\bar{x}\).

title: 4  Descriptive Stats IV
text:
4.10 Check Your Understanding
Test the main ideas of the chapter before moving on to the exercises. Pick an answer to see whether you are right and why.

What is the range of \(x=\{12, 7, 25, 3, 18\}\)?

\(25\)
\(22\)
\(13\)
\(15\)


Range \(=\) Maximum \(-\) Minimum \(=25-3=22\). It uses only the two extreme values.



Why does the variance square the deviations from the mean?

To express dispersion in the original units
To make the measure resistant to outliers
Because the raw deviations always add up to zero
To give every observation the same deviation


Positive and negative deviations cancel exactly around the mean. Squaring makes every deviation positive. The cost is that the variance is in squared units and is sensitive to large deviations.



Treating \(x=\{2, 4, 6\}\) as a sample, what is the sample variance \(s^2\)?

\(4\)
\(2.67\)
\(8\)
\(2\)


The mean is \(4\), the squared deviations are \(4\), \(0\), and \(4\), and their sum is \(8\). Dividing by \(n-1=2\) gives \(s^2=4\). Dividing by \(n=3\) would give the population formula, \(2.67\).



The variance of a product’s price is \(2{,}500\) dollars squared. What is the standard deviation?

$2,500
$1,250
$25
$50


The standard deviation is the square root of the variance, \(\sqrt{2{,}500}=50\), which brings the measure back to dollars.



What is the mean absolute deviation of \(x=\{2, 4, 6\}\) (using \(n\) in the denominator)?

\(2\)
\(4\)
\(1.33\)
\(0\)


The absolute deviations from the mean of \(4\) are \(2\), \(0\), and \(2\). Their average is \(4/3\approx1.33\). The sample standard deviation, \(2\), is larger because squaring amplifies large deviations.



Stock A has a mean price of $10 and a standard deviation of $2. Stock B has a mean price of $200 and a standard deviation of $20. Which stock is more variable relative to its price?

Stock A, with a CV of \(20\%\) versus \(10\%\)
Stock B, because its standard deviation is larger
They vary the same, since both CVs are equal
They cannot be compared because the means differ


\(CV_A=(2/10)\times100=20\%\) and \(CV_B=(20/200)\times100=10\%\). The CV removes the effect of scale, so we can compare the two.



Fund X has a mean return of \(9\%\) and a standard deviation of \(12\%\). Fund Y has a mean return of \(6\%\) and a standard deviation of \(4\%\). The risk-free rate is \(2\%\). Which fund has the better risk-adjusted performance?

Fund X, because its mean return is higher
Fund X, with a Sharpe ratio of \(0.75\)
They are equal
Fund Y, with a Sharpe ratio of \(1.00\)


Fund X: \((9-2)/12\approx0.58\). Fund Y: \((6-2)/4=1.00\). Fund Y earns more excess return per unit of risk.



Stock names are in column B and returns in column C. Which formula returns the standard deviation of AAPL returns only?

=STDEVIF(C:C, B:B, "AAPL")
=STDEV(IF(B2:B1189="AAPL", C2:C1189))
=STDEV.S(B:B, "AAPL")
=VAR.S(IF(B2:B1189="AAPL", C2:C1189))


Excel has no STDEVIF function, so we combine STDEV with IF in an array formula. The VAR.S(IF(...)) formula returns the variance, not the standard deviation.

title: 5  Descriptive Stats V
text:
5.12 Check Your Understanding
Test the main ideas of the chapter before moving on to the exercises. Pick an answer to see whether you are right and why.

By Chebyshev’s theorem, what share of any data set lies within \(4\) standard deviations of the mean?

Exactly \(93.75\%\)
At least \(75\%\)
At least \(93.75\%\)
About \(99.7\%\)


\(1-1/4^2=1-1/16=0.9375\). Chebyshev gives a minimum share that holds for any distribution, not an exact value.



Exam scores are bell shaped with a mean of \(50\) and a standard deviation of \(5\). According to the empirical rule, about what share of scores fall between \(40\) and \(60\)?

About \(68\%\)
About \(99.7\%\)
At least \(75\%\)
About \(95\%\)


\(40\) and \(60\) are two standard deviations from the mean, so the empirical rule gives about \(95\%\). Chebyshev’s guarantee of at least \(75\%\) is also true but much less precise for bell-shaped data.



Exam scores have a mean of \(70\) and a standard deviation of \(8\). What is the z-score of a score of \(90\), and is it a suspected outlier?

\(z=2.5\); a suspected outlier
\(z=2.5\); not a suspected outlier
\(z=20\); a suspected outlier
\(z=-2.5\); not a suspected outlier


\(z=(90-70)/8=2.5\). The score is \(2.5\) standard deviations above the mean, which is unusual but within the \(|z| \le 3\) cutoff.



A sorted data set has \(n=11\) values. Using \(L_p=1+k(n-1)\), where is the \(30\)th percentile located?

At position \(4\)
At position \(3.3\)
At position \(3.6\)
At position \(30\)


\(L_{30}=1+0.30(11-1)=4\), so the \(30\)th percentile is the fourth value in the sorted data. This is the method used by PERCENTILE.INC.



A data set has \(Q_1=20\) and \(Q_3=30\). Using the IQR method, which of these values is an outlier?

\(44\)
\(6\)
\(30\)
\(48\)


\(IQR=30-20=10\). The limits are \(20-1.5(10)=5\) and \(30+1.5(10)=45\). Only \(48\) falls outside \([5,45]\).



Household incomes in a city are mostly moderate, with a few very high incomes. What skewness would you expect?

Negative (left-skewed)
Positive (right-skewed)
Zero (symmetric)
It cannot be positive for incomes


A few very large values create a long right tail. Their large positive cubed z-scores dominate the sum, so \(Sk>0\).



The daily returns of an asset have an excess kurtosis of \(K=2.5\). What does this tell you?

The returns are leptokurtic: extreme returns are more common than under a normal distribution
The returns are platykurtic: extreme returns are rare
The returns are mesokurtic
The returns are skewed to the left


\(K>0\) means heavier tails than the normal distribution. Kurtosis describes the tails, not the direction of asymmetry, which is measured by skewness.



Which Excel formula returns the third quartile, \(Q_3\)?

=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 0.75)
=PERCENTILE.INC(A:A, 75)
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 3)
=QUARTILE.INC(A:A, 4)


The quart argument takes the values \(0\) through \(4\), and \(3\) returns \(Q_3\). PERCENTILE.INC(A:A, 0.75) also works, since its k is a decimal. The argument \(4\) returns the maximum.
